title: Though He Slay Me: Job Prepares His Case
summary: Job tells his friends they are worthless physicians who lie on God's behalf, and warns that God will judge them for it. Then he resolves to take his case to God directly, at the risk of his life, confident that he will be vindicated. He asks God to lift his hand and stop terrifying him, to show him his sins, and to explain why he treats Job as an enemy.
story: This is the middle of Job's long reply to Zophar and to all three friends (chapters 12 to 14). In chapter 12 he dismissed their claim to superior wisdom. Here he turns from them entirely. The idea of a lawsuit with God, which in chapter 9 seemed hopeless, becomes a decision: “Behold, now that I have prepared my case, I know that I will be vindicated” (verse 18). This is a turning point in Job's thinking. He is no longer only lamenting; he is pressing for a hearing. The same resolve will grow through chapter 23 and reach its formal end in the oath of chapter 31. When God finally answers in chapter 38, he will answer the man who asked for this hearing.
historical:
The chapter's setting is the same undated world of Uz as the rest of the dialogue, and its interest lies less in historical events than in ancient legal practice and ancient ideas of speaking about God. In Israel and neighboring societies, cases were heard before elders or judges. Each side arranged its case, a legal term Job uses in verse 18, meaning to set out one's arguments in order, much as soldiers are drawn up in ranks. Witnesses were expected to tell the truth, and a false witness could face the penalty he had sought for the accused (Deuteronomy 19:16-19).

Job applies that principle to his friends. They are acting as God's advocates, and in doing so they are shading the truth to defend him. Job warns that God does not want such a defense and will expose it (verses 7-11). It is a remarkable claim for the ancient world, where defending the gods was normally thought to please them.
cultural:
The image of worthless physicians (verse 4) draws on ancient medicine, which combined practical remedies such as ointments and plasters with prayers and ritual. The word translated smear suggests plastering over, as if the friends are covering the wound with lies instead of treating it. Their maxims, Job says, are proverbs of ashes, and their defenses are defenses of clay (verse 12): sayings that crumble, like a fortification made of mud brick.

Taking one's life in one's hands (verse 14) was a vivid idiom for exposing oneself to mortal danger. The first half of the line, literally taking one's flesh in one's teeth, likely pictures an animal carrying its prey and risking losing it. Ancient people also held that no one could see God and live (compare Exodus 33:20), and Job knows that approaching God's face is dangerous. Stocks for the feet (verse 27) were wooden restraints used to hold prisoners, and marking the soles of the feet may refer to branding or tracking slaves and prisoners, though the exact meaning is uncertain.
literary: The chapter has two halves joined at a hinge. Verses 1-12 address the friends: Job claims equal knowledge, says he wants to speak with God rather than with them, and accuses them of lying for God. Verses 13-19 are the hinge, Job's decision to speak whatever the cost, including the famous verse 15. Verses 20-28 address God directly, with two requests (verses 20-22), a demand to know his sins (verse 23), and a lament over being treated as an enemy (verses 24-28). Legal vocabulary runs through the whole: argue, plea, case, vindicate, indict, call, answer, record, accusations. The chapter ends with a quiet image of human decay, a moth-eaten garment, that leads into the meditation on human frailty in chapter 14.

outline.t: Job knows what they know; they should be silent
Will you lie on God's behalf?
Job resolves to present his case to God
Two requests, and a plea to know his sin

doctrines.note: Job insists that God does not need defending with falsehoods. Speaking of God must be truthful, even when the truth is uncomfortable. False comfort offered in God's name is a sin against him.
Verse 15 shows faith that clings to God even while God seems to be the source of the pain. Job's hope is not in escaping God but in appearing before him.
Job says that his salvation lies in being able to appear before God at all, since the godless cannot (verse 16). He believes that standing before God's face is itself the way of rescue.

words.note: Yakach, to argue, reason, or decide a case. It appears four times in the chapter: Job wants to argue his case before God (verse 3), God will rebuke the friends (verse 10), and Job will defend his ways to God's face (verse 15). The same verb gave the arbiter of 9:33.

Yachal, to wait or hope. In verse 15 it is the verb behind I will hope in Him. It describes patient, expectant waiting, often for God. The verse's exact wording is debated, as the hard question below explains.

Yeshuah, salvation, deliverance, or rescue. In verse 16 Job says this, his coming before God, will be his salvation. The word comes from the same root as the Hebrew name Yeshua (Joshua), from which the name Jesus is derived.

Mashal, proverb, saying, or comparison. It is the word behind the book of Proverbs. Job calls the friends' sayings proverbs of ashes (verse 12), wisdom that looks like wisdom but has no substance left in it.

christ: Job's resolve to go before God's face and be vindicated has a thematic echo in the story of Jesus. Jesus entrusted himself to the one who judges justly while he suffered unjustly (1 Peter 2:23), and his last words from the cross in Luke are a psalm of trust, “Father, into Your hands I commit My spirit” (Luke 23:46, drawing on Psalm 31:5). The resurrection is presented in the New Testament as God's vindication of the righteous sufferer (Acts 2:23-24; 1 Timothy 3:16). Job's confidence that he will be vindicated before God points toward the Christian hope that believers, too, can approach God's throne with confidence because of Christ (Hebrews 4:16). None of this is predicted in Job; it is where the longing he voices finally leads.

hard.q: Does verse 15 say “I will hope in Him” or “I have no hope”?
hard.a: The famous line, “Though He slay me, I will hope in Him,” rests on a small textual difference. The Hebrew consonants written in the traditional text (called the ketiv, what is written) spell the word lo, meaning not, which would give something like: he will slay me; I have no hope, yet I will defend my ways to his face. Jewish scribes also preserved a reading to be spoken aloud (the qere, what is read), which spells lo differently, meaning to him or in him, giving the familiar I will hope in him. Both words sound the same in Hebrew. Many ancient versions and most English translations follow the spoken reading, and many modern scholars and some translations prefer the written one. On either reading, Job is going before God to argue his case with no guarantee of survival. The difference is whether that act is described as hope or as defiance, and the rest of the chapter, in which Job expects to be vindicated (verse 18), is often cited in support of hope.

questions: Job accuses his friends of lying on God's behalf. In what ways are people tempted to defend God with half-truths, and why does Job think God is offended by it?
“Though He slay me, I will hope in Him.” What would it look like for you to trust God in a situation where he seems to be the problem?
Job asks God to show him his sins. Have you ever wanted to know why something was happening so badly that you would have accepted an accusation? What does that desire reveal?
